claims.text: Controlled post-deposition annealing reduces defect density in as-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys.
Controlled post-deposition annealing reduces microstructural inhomogeneities in these alloys.
Defects and microstructural inhomogeneities pin the advancing phase boundary during the first-order magnetostructural transition.
Reducing phase-boundary pinning moderates hysteresis.
Reducing phase-boundary pinning broadens the magnetocaloric response.
The as-deposited alloy is in an ordered, single-phase hexagonal state.
The as-deposited alloy exhibits a sharp first-order magnetostructural transition with pronounced hysteresis.
Annealing at approximately 700 degrees Celsius for 1 hour is the proposed controlled intervention.
Annealing relaxes internal stresses in the alloy.
Relaxation of internal stresses and reduction of defects lower the energy barriers for nucleation and growth of the magnetic/structural phase.
Lower nucleation-and-growth barriers produce a smoother and less abrupt magnetostructural transition.
The smoother transition reduces hysteresis and broadens the temperature range over which the magnetocaloric effect is significant.
Annealed samples will have lower hysteresis than otherwise identical as-deposited samples during low-field magnetic-cooling cycles.
Annealed samples will have a broader magnetocaloric-response profile than otherwise identical as-deposited samples.
Annealing may slightly diminish the peak magnetic entropy change while improving reversibility and reducing hysteretic losses.
The as-deposited samples have limited heat-exchange efficacy because of their lower surface-to-volume ratio.
The predicted annealing effect is limited to conditions that reduce defects without causing phase decomposition or loss of mechanical stability.
The predictions are intended to apply under applied magnetic fields below 2 tesla and in the absence of severe plastic deformation.
A comparison of composition-matched as-deposited and annealed samples, with magnetocaloric testing and XRD/TEM characterization, can test the proposed defect-mediated mechanism.
Failure of annealing to change defect indicators or reduce hysteresis, including retention of an equally sharp and hysteretic response, is specified as falsifying the hypothesis.
